title: How to Bake Sourdough-Based Pizza Crust for a Crowd
meta_description: Learn how to master a large batch sourdough pizza night. Get professional tips on dough scaling, cold fermentation, and easy cleanup for your crowd.
html:
There is something inherently satisfying about a sourdough pizza party. Between the tangy crust and the bubbly char, it feels more like an event than a meal. But if you’ve only ever made a single loaf of sourdough bread, scaling up for a group can feel intimidating. The key to a successful large batch sourdough pizza session is all in the timing and the surface area.

When you're feeding six to ten people, you can't just wing it. You need a system that allows the dough to develop flavor without taking over your entire kitchen counter. Here is how to streamline the process from starter to slice.

Scaling Your Starter for a Large Batch Sourdough Pizza

The biggest bottleneck in sourdough baking is the starter. Most home bakers keep a small jar of starter, but for a crowd, you'll need a significant amount of active, bubbly leaven. To avoid a mid-prep panic, start your "build" 24 hours before you plan to mix the dough.

If you need 500g of active starter for your batch, feed your starter the night before so you have at least 600g available. This ensures you have enough for the recipe plus enough left over to maintain your culture. Use a large glass bowl or a plastic Cambro container; sourdough expands quickly, and there is nothing more frustrating than a floury explosion in your fridge at 3 AM.

The Master Dough Formula and Bulk Fermentation

For a large batch, I recommend a high-hydration dough (around 65-70%) to ensure the crust stays airy even if your home oven doesn't reach 900 degrees. Mix your flour, water, salt, and active starter in a large mixing tub. Use the "stretch and fold" method every 30 minutes for the first two hours to build strength without needing a commercial mixer.

Once the dough has grown by about 50%, move to the division phase. Instead of letting one giant mass of dough ferment, weigh out individual portions (usually 250g to 300g per pizza) and place them into lightly oiled individual containers. This prevents the dough from over-proofing in the center of a large mass and makes the logistics of a party much easier.

The Secret to Flavor: Cold Fermentation

If you want that professional, artisanal taste, do not bake your dough the same day you mix it. Place your individual dough balls in the refrigerator for 24 to 72 hours. This slow cold ferment breaks down the starches, making the crust more digestible and developing those signature sourdough bubbles.

On the day of the party, take the dough out of the fridge about two hours before baking. This allows the gluten to relax, making the dough much easier to stretch by hand. If the dough is too cold, it will snap back like a rubber band, leaving you with a thick, dense crust instead of a light, airy one.

Baking and Managing the Cleanup

Most home kitchens lack a dedicated pizza oven, which means we rely on baking sheets or pizza stones. When you're pumping out multiple pizzas for a crowd, the risk of sticking is high. This is where the right gear makes the difference. I always line my sheets with Silicone Baking Mats.

Unlike parchment paper, which can curl or burn at high temperatures, Silicone Baking Mats provide a consistent, non-stick surface that ensures even heat distribution across the bottom of the crust. They are a lifesaver for a large batch sourdough pizza night because you can slide the pizza off easily and skip the dreaded scrubbing of burnt-on flour and cheese. Just wipe them down and they're ready for the next pie.

Tips for a Smooth Pizza Assembly Line

To keep the host from spending the whole night in the kitchen, set up a station. Arrange your toppings in small bowls and keep your sauce and cheese within arm's reach. Here is the ideal workflow:

  • Prep: Grate the cheese and slice the toppings before the guests arrive.
  • Stretch: Shape the dough on a floured surface, then move it to the mat.
  • Top: Keep toppings light; too much sauce will make a sourdough crust soggy.
  • Bake: Use the highest setting on your oven (usually 500°F) and rotate the pans halfway through.

FAQ

Can I freeze my sourdough pizza dough balls?

Yes! After the initial bulk fermentation, you can freeze individual dough balls in freezer-safe bags. Thaw them in the refrigerator for 24 hours before the day you plan to bake.

What if my dough is too sticky to handle?

Sourdough can be tacky. Instead of adding more flour—which can make the crust tough—wet your hands with water. This prevents the dough from sticking to your skin while you're shaping it.

How do I get a crispier bottom without a pizza stone?

Preheat your baking sheet in the oven before sliding your pizza (and its Silicone Baking Mat) onto it. The initial hit of heat helps sear the bottom of the crust for a better crunch.
